chapter: Reel 2: Los Angeles musicians, the Apex and Cotton Club
title: Sitting in with white bands at the Cotton Club
summary: Howard confirms he sat in with white bands as a guest for a tune or two, with no mixed steady jobs then.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You mentioned something, the first time I came out, about you setting in with white bands at the Cotton Club or something. Do you remember anything about that?
Oh, yeah.
How did that work, because at that time I'm pretty sure --
Fine, beautiful.
Who did you set in with? Do you remember any of those bands?
I can't think of them, name them.

It's like you had gone to the Cotton Club, and maybe it wasn't Jimmy Dorsey, but somebody that was a big leader, and you were able to come in and set in with them for a number or two. Do you remember that?
No, I don't remember. Can't remember the names.
You remember the experience, though.
Yeah.
I mean, because you couldn't actually
sit in with the bands all the time, it just had to be like a guest (inaudible) for a couple of tunes.
That's right.
And, way, you just sort of had to go off to the side and wait until --
Come to (inaudible) place and come back and play again. Like, get back and play something that they wanted to play, that I could play.
So the musicians seemed to accept you very well. It's just that it wasn't being done, where blacks and whites were working together on steady job.
No. Wasn't no blacks and whites working together at steady jobs then at those times. They didn't do that.
They didn't do that. But the musicians were fine, they didn't seem to --
They didn't bother.
Or say anything.
